https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A resolution of the Troy Board of Education certifying an Operating Millage Renewal Proposal to the Oakland County Clerk for the November 5, 2024 election. Adopted at a special meeting held June 6, 2024 at 5 p.m. and certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary. Michigan election law required certification no later than **4:00 p.m. on August 13, 2024**.

What the proposal actually asks
The ballot language asks whether the tax limitation may be **increased in the amount of 22 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy**, of which **not more than 5.7049 mills may be imposed on principal residences**, for twenty years — the years 2026 to 2045 inclusive.

The gap between 22 authorized and 18 leviable is the point. The explanatory paragraph states the proposal would renew the authority expiring with the 2025 tax levy, restrict the principal-residence levy, and **"protect against the impact of Headlee rollbacks of up to 4.0 mills."** The recital is equally direct: the Board determined it necessary to renew the authority *and* "increase the prior authority to protect against the impact of future rollbacks under the Headlee Amendment."

What it means in practice
The district continues to levy the statutory 18.00 mills on non-homestead property — principally industrial, commercial and residential rental — and on principal residences levies only the portion needed to receive the full per-pupil foundation allowance. The proposal notes the district **only levied 2.7936 mills on principal residences in 2024**, well under the 5.7049 ceiling being authorized.

Estimated revenue: **$42.5 million during the 2026 calendar year**.

Mechanics
The Secretary and Superintendent are each individually authorized to file the resolution and any required forms. Notably, clause 2 authorizes them to **update the Proposal before submission to reflect any Headlee rollbacks applicable to the 2024 operating millage** — the numbers were not final at adoption. The Election Coordinator is directed to post and publish notice of the last day of registration and of the election, and to have ballots prepared in the Exhibit A form.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the resolution certifying the Operating Millage Renewal Proposal to the November 5, 2024 ballot, adopted by the Troy Board of Education at a special meeting held in the School District on June 6, 2024 at 5 p.m. local time. The certifying officer is Gary Hauff, Secretary of the Board, who also certifies that the meeting was conducted and noticed in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267 of the Public Acts of Michigan 1976.

The recitals set out the purpose with unusual candor. The Board has determined that it is necessary for the continued operation of the School District **to renew the authority to levy certain operating mills and increase the prior authority to protect against the impact of future rollbacks under the Headlee Amendment**, as described in the Proposal attached as Exhibit A. It is necessary and desirable to submit the Proposal to the electors at an election on November 5, 2024, and in order to do so the Board must certify the Proposal to the Clerk of the County of Oakland — the School District Election Coordinator — as required by Michigan election law not later than 4:00 p.m. on August 13, 2024.

The operative clauses are four. First, the Proposal is certified to the Election Coordinator and the local clerks for submission on the November election date, with the Secretary of the Board and the Superintendent each individually authorized and directed to file the resolution and complete any forms, certificates or documents required to evidence the certification by the August 13 deadline. Second — and worth noting — the Secretary or Superintendent are further authorized, prior to submission, **to update the Proposal to reflect any Headlee rollbacks applicable to the current operating millage for the 2024 year**, meaning the millage figures in the certified language were expected to move between June and August. Third, the Election Coordinator is authorized and directed to post and publish notice of the last day of registration and notice of election, and to have ballots prepared and printed in the Exhibit A form or stated as a proposal on the voting machines, which may include other matters presented to the electorate on the same date. Fourth, conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

Exhibit A contains the ballot language itself, in two parts.

The explanatory paragraph states that the proposal would renew the authority of the School District, **which expires with the 2025 tax levy**, to levy up to 18.00 mills for general school district operating purposes on taxable property not exempt from the levy; would **restrict the levy on principal residences (owner-occupied homes) to no more than 5.7049 mills**; and would **protect against the impact of Headlee rollbacks of up to 4.0 mills**. It explains that this authorization would allow the district to continue to levy the statutory limit of 18.00 mills on non-homestead property — principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property — and to continue to levy on principal residence property only that portion of the mills necessary to allow the district to receive the full revenue per pupil foundation allowance permitted by the State. It closes with a concrete reassurance to homeowners: **the School District only levied 2.7936 mills on principal residences in 2024**, against the 5.7049 ceiling being authorized.

The question put to voters reads: shall the limitation on the amount of taxes which may be imposed on taxable property in the Troy School District be **increased in the amount of 22 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy** ($18.00 per $1,000 of taxable value), to the extent such property is not statutorily exempt, and of which **not more than 5.7049 mills may be imposed on principal residences**, for **twenty (20) years, the years 2026 to 2045, inclusive**, to provide funds for operating expenses of the School District? The language states the operating millage, if approved and levied, would provide **estimated revenues to the School District of $42.5 million during the 2026 calendar year**, to be used for general operating purposes.

The structure is the standard Michigan device for defending an 18-mill non-homestead levy against Headlee erosion. Because Article IX Section 31 of the Michigan Constitution rolls back millage rates when a taxing unit's taxable value grows faster than inflation, a district authorized at exactly 18 mills loses revenue permanently each time a rollback bites — and unlike most local units, a school district cannot make up an 18-mill shortfall from the State, because the foundation allowance formula assumes the full 18 mills is collected. Authorizing 22 mills while capping the levy at 18 creates a 4-mill cushion that absorbs rollbacks without reducing what is actually levied. The companion PFM analysis presented to the Board in February 2024 quantifies exactly what that cushion is worth: at the district's 5-year average millage reduction fraction of 0.9882, a 4-mill buffer still fails in year 16 and accumulates $5,902,057 of lost state aid over twenty years, while a 5-mill buffer holds until year 20 and loses only $204,424 — which is the analytical basis for asking for a cushion at all, and for the size chosen.

What it is
Agenda item 8.A. at the March 19, 2024 meeting — "Troy SD 2024 Operating Millage Analysis," prepared by PFM Financial Advisors LLC (555 Briarwood Circle, Suite 333, Ann Arbor) and dated February 20, 2024. Source data is the Oakland Equalization Department and the district's historical L-4029 forms.

Historical operating millage, 2004–2023
The total operating levy held at 18.0000 mills in almost every year, but the composition shifted. From 2004 through 2013 the district levied the full 18.0000 as "Operating Millage" with zero "Hedge Millage." From 2014 the hedge appears and grows as the operating component erodes:

| Year | Operating | Hedge | Total | MRF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 16.9612 | 1.0388 | 18.0000 | 1.0000 |
| 2022 | 16.9612 | 1.0388 | 18.0000 | 0.9693 |
| 2021 | 17.4984 | 0.5016 | 18.0000 | 0.9919 |
| 2020 | 17.6413 | 0.3587 | 18.0000 | 0.9954 |
| 2019 | 17.7228 | 0.2772 | 18.0000 | 0.9846 |

Millage reduction fraction averages: **0.9882 over 5 years**, 0.9916 over 10, 0.9944 over 15, 0.9958 over 20. The 2022 fraction of 0.9693 is the sharpest single-year rollback in the twenty-year record.

The modelled loss
Estimated loss in annual state aid funding from projected operating millage rollback, over twenty levy years 2026–2045:

| Scenario | Cumulative loss |
|---|---|
| 4.0000-mill buffer, 0.9900 rollback | **$526,140** |
| 4.0000-mill buffer, 0.9882 rollback | **$5,902,057** |
| 5.0000-mill buffer, 0.9882 rollback | **$204,424** |

The shape matters as much as the totals. Under every scenario the loss is exactly zero for the first fifteen years — the buffer absorbs the rollback entirely. The 4-mill/0.9882 case first shows loss in 2041 at $51,133, then climbs steeply: $600,253, $1,164,721, $1,744,877, $2,341,072. The 4-mill/0.9900 case doesn't break until 2044. The 5-mill case doesn't break until 2045.

Assumptions
Estimated 2023 equivalent non-PRE taxable value of **$1,722,654,355**; annual growth in non-PRE taxable value of 5% in 2024 and 2% thereafter; constant millage reduction fractions as stated, with the note that actual MRF will vary each year. The analysis explicitly **does not include the effect on Hold Harmless millage**.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is agenda item 8.A. at the Troy Board of Education meeting of March 19, 2024: the 2024 Operating Millage Analysis prepared by PFM Financial Advisors LLC, dated February 20, 2024. PFM's Ann Arbor office is given as 555 Briarwood Circle, Suite 333, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48108. The same firm serves as the district's municipal advisor on bond issues. It is a five-page technical exhibit whose function is to price the Headlee problem, and it is the analytical foundation for the operating millage renewal proposal the Board certified to the November 2024 ballot three months later.

The first exhibit is the historical operating millage levied by the district, sourced from the Oakland Equalization Department and the district's historical L-4029 forms. It shows four columns per year: operating millage levied, hedge millage levied, total operating levy, and the Headlee millage reduction fraction.

From 2004 through 2013 the district levied a flat 18.0000 mills of operating millage with 0.0000 of hedge, and a millage reduction fraction of 1.0000 in every year — no rollback. The pattern breaks in 2014, when the total levy dips to 17.8920 with an MRF of 0.9940, and 2015 at 17.8794 with 0.9993. 2016 returns to 18.0000 at 1.0000. In 2017 a hedge component appears for the first time — 17.6742 operating plus 0.3258 hedge to reach 18.0000 — with an MRF of 0.9819. 2018 returns to 18.0000/0.0000/1.0000. From 2019 the hedge becomes permanent and grows: 2019 at 17.7228 + 0.2772 with MRF 0.9846; 2020 at 17.6413 + 0.3587 with 0.9954; 2021 at 17.4984 + 0.5016 with 0.9919; 2022 at 16.9612 + 1.0388 with **0.9693**, the sharpest rollback in the twenty-year record; and 2023 holding at 16.9612 + 1.0388 with an MRF of 1.0000.

The rolling averages of the millage reduction fraction are given at the right of the table: **0.9882 as the 5-year average** (anchored at 2019), 0.9916 as the 10-year (at 2014), 0.9944 as the 15-year (at 2009) and 0.9958 as the 20-year (at 2004). The trend is unambiguous — rollbacks have accelerated, and the recent average is materially worse than the long-run average.

The second exhibit models the consequence. PFM summarizes the estimated reduction in State Aid due to the projected impact of Headlee millage reduction fraction rollbacks on a school's non-PRE operating millage revenues, under three scenarios: a 4-mill buffer with an MRF of 0.9900, a 4-mill buffer with an MRF of 0.9882 (the 5-year average), and a 5-mill buffer with an MRF of 0.9882 — each run over twenty levy years, 2026 through 2045.

The results table shows zero loss in every scenario for levy years 1 through 15 (2026 through 2040). The buffer absorbs the entire rollback for fifteen years in all three cases. The divergence comes at the tail. Under a 4-mill buffer at 0.9882, loss first appears in year 16 (2041) at $51,133, then $600,253 in 2042, $1,164,721 in 2043, $1,744,877 in 2044 and $2,341,072 in 2045 — **a cumulative $5,902,057**. Under a 4-mill buffer at the slightly gentler 0.9900 rate, nothing is lost until year 19 (2044) at $16,254, then $509,886 in 2045, for a cumulative **$526,140**. Under a 5-mill buffer at 0.9882, nothing is lost until the final year, 2045, at $204,424, which is also the cumulative total.

The comparison is the argument: moving from a 4-mill to a 5-mill buffer at the district's actual recent rollback rate reduces twenty-year exposure from $5.9 million to about $200,000. Equally, the difference between assuming 0.9882 and 0.9900 — a gap of 0.0018 in the fraction — swings the 4-mill outcome by $5.4 million, which is a fair measure of how sensitive the projection is to an assumption nobody controls.

The third exhibit is the detailed year-by-year calculation behind the 4-mill/0.9882 case, showing for each levy year the non-homestead taxable value, its growth rate, the prior-year rate, the Headlee factor, the resulting current millage, the same three columns for the 4-mill buffer maximum, the estimated non-homestead millage to be levied, the remaining buffer, and the estimated revenue loss at equivalent non-homestead taxable value.

The mechanics are visible in the numbers. Taxable value starts at $1,722,654,355 in 2023 and grows to $2,741,517,691 by 2045. The operating rate and the buffer maximum both decay at 0.9882 per year in lockstep — the operating rate from 18.0000 through 17.7876, 17.5777, 17.3703 and onward to 14.0286; the buffer from 4.0000 through 3.9528, 3.9062, 3.8601 and onward to 3.1175. Because both decay together, the sum available (rate plus buffer) stays at or above 18.0000 through 2040, so the district can still levy the full 18.0000 and the "estimated loss" column reads zero. In 2041 the sum falls to 17.9798 — the first year the combined authorization can no longer reach 18 mills — and the loss column turns positive at $51,133. From there the shortfall widens each year as both components continue to decay: 17.7676 in 2042, 17.5580 in 2043, 17.3508 in 2044, and 17.1461 in 2045.

The assumptions are restated on both the summary and detail pages: estimated 2023 equivalent non-PRE taxable value of $1,722,654,355; annual growth in non-PRE taxable value of 5% in 2024 and 2% thereafter; constant Headlee rollback millage reduction fractions as noted, with the explicit caveat that actual MRF will vary each year; and that the analysis **does not include the effect on Hold Harmless millage** — a material exclusion, since Troy is a hold-harmless district whose homestead levy moves with the same forces. Both pages carry the note that the tables are for informational purposes only.

The resolving clause amends and approves the general appropriations and budget for fiscal year 2023-24 for those funds, at Food Service Fund $6,060,793, Community Service Fund $2,101,071 and Troy School District Preschool Fund $3,715,667.

The Food Service Fund is amended as follows. On the revenue side, local falls $11,709 to $431,791; state rises $89,916 to $5,339,916; federal is unchanged at $687,000; and incoming transfers remain nil. Total revenue rises $78,207 to $6,458,707. The July 1 fund balance is restated upward by $211,268 to $3,015,211 — the prior year having closed better than assumed — making total available to appropriate $9,473,918, up $289,475. The Community Service Fund is amended with the sharpest adverse movement of the three. Local revenue falls $43,000 to $1,970,000, with federal and incoming transfers both nil, so total revenues and incoming transfers fall $43,000 to $1,970,000. The July 1 fund balance is restated **down** $131,017 to $2,326,059, making total available to appropriate $4,296,059, a reduction of $174,017. Community Services expenditure rises $262,497 to $2,101,071, with debt service and outgoing transfers nil. The combined effect flips the fund from a projected $174,426 surplus to a $(131,071) deficit, a swing of $305,497, and the projected June 30 balance falls $436,514 from $2,631,502 to $2,194,988. This is the Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2024-25, filed at the Troy Board of Education meeting of June 20, 2024. MHSAA's address is given as 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, telephone (517) 332-5046. It is the direct predecessor of the 2025-26 resolution filed a year later as agenda item 6E, and the two are textually identical apart from dates and the completed enrollment entries.

The preamble describes the MHSAA as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation comprised of public, private and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose Boards of Education or Governing Bodies have voluntarily applied for and received membership on behalf of their secondary schools. The association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules for participation in them. Each board wishing to host or participate must join the MHSAA and agree to abide by and enforce its rules, regulations and qualifications concerning eligibility, game rules and tournament policies, procedures and schedules. It is a condition for participation in any MHSAA postseason tournament that high schools adhere to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports.

A proprietary-rights paragraph states that MHSAA tournaments are the collective property of the association and not of any individual member school, and that the MHSAA reserves the right to promote and advance the membership's interests through publication information; exclusive arrangements creating recognition and exposure for school-sponsored activities; restrictive policies prohibiting exploitation and commercialization of MHSAA-sponsored tournaments; appropriate proprietary interests; and the use of images or transmissions identifying contest officials, spectators and member schools' students, personnel and marks.

Two procedural conditions constrain the Board. The resolution must be formally ratified and properly signed, with one signed copy returned to MHSAA and one retained — and the instructions state plainly that "Resolutions that are modified in any way or are supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on MHSAA membership or tournament participation shall be rejected." The authorization is effective from August 1, 2024 until July 31, 2025, "during which the authorization may not be revoked." Together these make membership a take-it-or-leave-it annual commitment.

The operative resolution enrolls the named schools, under the direction of the adopting board, as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc., and further enrolls them to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities the association sponsors. The Board delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for supervision and control of those activities; accepts the Constitution and By-Laws of the association; and adopts as its own the rules, regulations and interpretations published in the current Handbook as minimum standards governing the conduct of its interscholastic athletics program, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools hosting or participating in the association's meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures and schedules.

A Record of Adoption block captures the school names, the day and month of adoption in 2024, and signature lines for the governing body name, the Board Secretary or designee, address, city and zip code, and contact email, with completed forms to be saved and emailed to camala@mhsaa.com as an attachment.

The reverse side lists the schools to be MHSAA members during 2024-25, separated into member high schools and member junior high/middle schools, with the instruction that middle schools be listed separately from high schools even where all grades are housed in the same building. Membership eligibility under the MHSAA Constitution requires that a school building have enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students — whether for grades 6 through 8 or 9, grades 7 through 8 or 9, or grades 9 or 10 through 12 — and, if nonpublic, that the school qualify for federal income tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. To reach the fifteen-student minimum for middle school membership, schools may join the MHSAA at the 6th-grade level whether or not 6th-grade students participate in athletics.

Two qualifications follow. The section does not require school districts to become member schools at the junior high or middle school level, nor to sponsor any interscholastic athletics for 6th-grade students. But if a district's membership resolution lists a junior high or middle school as a member, and that school sponsors a 6th-grade team in any sport or permits a 6th-grade student to participate with 7th or 8th graders in any sport, then all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all sports involving 6th-graders on teams sponsored by that school. If the school does not allow any 6th-graders to participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.

The form is largely a blank template with fields for each member school's name, grade configuration, anticipated 7th and 8th grade enrollment, anticipated 6th grade enrollment, whether 6th-graders will participate in at least one sport with 7th and 8th graders, and which grade levels are covered by membership. Two entries are completed in this filing. **Larson Middle School** is listed with an anticipated 2024-25 7th and 8th grade enrollment of 484 and 6th grade enrollment of 287. **Smith Middle School** appears as entry 4 among the junior high and middle schools, with a grade configuration of 6-8, anticipated 7th and 8th grade enrollment of 432, anticipated 6th grade enrollment of 202, and membership grade levels marked for 6, 7 and 8.

Read against the 2025-26 resolution filed a year later, the enrollment figures show Smith Middle School's 7th and 8th grade cohort falling from 432 to 419 and its 6th grade from 202 to 184 — consistent with the district-wide enrollment decline the June 2024 budget presentation projected at 12,370 to 12,300 to 12,200 FTE.
